opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
This line from the Book of Hosea 14:3 It sits inside one of the most beautiful repentance prayers in the Old Testament.
“Assyria will not save us;
We will not ride on horses.
We shall say no more, ‘Our God,’ to the work of our hands;
For in you the orphan finds compassion.”

“The work of our hands” refers to idols people made themselves—wood, metal, wealth, power, alliances, anything they trusted instead of God. The line is essentially saying: We will stop calling the things we built or trusted in  ‘Our God’. This a moment of true humility.
The people finally recognize that the things they trusted in cannot save them. Earlier in the passage, they also say, “Assyria will not save us; we will not ride on horses.” In other words, political alliances, military strength, and human strategy are not the answer. 
Then the prayer ends with something striking: “for in you the orphan finds compassion.” In the ancient world, the orphan represented the most vulnerable person in society—someone with no protection, inheritance, or advocate. The people are essentially admitting that, without God, they are in the same position. They cannot secure their own future or rescue themselves.
That is the structure of real repentance in this passage: first, recognize the false things we trusted; second, renounce them; and finally, appeal to the mercy of God. And the remarkable part is what comes next. Immediately after this confession, God responds: “I will heal their defection; I will love them freely.”
So the movement of the passage is clear: idolatry, humility, and then restoration. The people stop trusting in what they made and return to the One whose compassion is greater than their failure.
For anyone who encounters this reading today, its meaning remains clear. The idols may look different—success, security, control, the things we build to protect ourselves—but the temptation is the same. What it reveals about us does not change with time: we still place our trust in what we can create or control. And yet the same truth remains—God’s compassion continues to meet the humble heart that turns back to Him.
